(NASDAQ:ENTA), a clinical stage biotechnology company dedicated to creating novel, small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases, today announced that data for zelicapavir, its oral, once-daily, N-protein inhibitor in development for the treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), will be presented at IDWeekTM 2026 being held October 21-24, 2026 virtually and at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center in Washington, DC. Details of the presentation are as follows: Poster Title: Zelicapavir Decreases Time to Complete RSV Symptom Resolution, Hospitalization and Viral Load in a Global, Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo (PBO)-Controlled Phase 2 Trial of High-Risk Adults Poster Session: Novel Agents Poster Number: 3 Date: Thursday October 22, 2026 Time: 12:15 PM - 1:30 PM ET Location: Poster Hall B-C Presenter: Christopher E. Harris, M.D. The poster will be available to view on the conference platform during the conference and on the Company’s website here. Further information about IDWeekTM 2026 can be found here. About Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. Enanta is using its robust, chemistry-driven approach and drug discovery capabilities to become a leader in the discovery and development of small molecule drugs for viral infections and immunological diseases. In virology, Enanta’s clinical programs are focused on the development of first-in-disease and best-in-disease treatments for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The Company’s immunology pipeline aims to develop treatments for inflammatory diseases by targeting key drivers of the type 2 immune response, with KIT, STAT6 and MRGPRX2 inhibition. Glecaprevir, a protease inhibitor discovered by Enanta, is part of the only treatment approved for curing both acute and chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and is sold by AbbVie in numerous countries under the tradenames MAVYRET® (U.S.) and MAVIRET® (ex-U.S.) (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). A portion of Enanta’s royalties from HCV products developed under its collaboration with AbbVie contribute ongoing funding to Enanta’s operations. Please visit www.enanta.com for more information. Wyoming Tribune Eagle/file Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save JACKSON — Dr. Travis Riddell spent most of his pediatric career treating babies hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus. Though the virus is extremely common, it can hit young babies hard, giving them bronchitis and outsized mucus. There’s no antiviral treatment for RSV, meaning doctors have to resort to purely supportive care. Parents around Jackson Hole may recall their infants getting sick with RSV as infants. Riddell certainly can. “My daughter, who’s now 10 years old, was in the ICU at St. John’s when she was 6 weeks old with RSV,” Riddell said. “So I’ve been there personally, on both sides of the bed.” But pediatricians have noticed a dramatic change over the last three years. In 2023, two protective RSV products — a vaccine for pregnant women and virus-fighting antibodies for infants — launched in the United States. That’s led to an outsized national decrease in RSV hospitalizations. “It really has been a game changer,” Dr. Jacqui Hardenbrook, a pediatrician at Paintbrush Pediatrics, said. “I think last winter, I only admitted two kids to the ICU.” Dr. Tiffany Milner, a pediatrician at St. John’s Health, recalls treating hospitals full of children with RSV when she started residency in Salt Lake City in 2009. That’s now changed dramatically. Across the country, RSV hospitalization dropped by as much as 71% in newborns after the shot became available, according to a 2025 study by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “It’s incredible,” Milner said. “It’s just so stressful as a new parent to care for a baby who is constantly coughing, and snot coming out of their nose, and having trouble feeding.” Mothers can protect their babies from RSV in two ways. They can receive a vaccine, which confers protection during their baby’s first six months of life. Babies younger than 8 months old also can receive nirsevimab or clesrovimab, which are antibodies. Antibodies are different from vaccines. Whereas vaccines contain parts of a virus — which train your body’s immune system to make antibodies that neutralize the virus — the antibody treatments fight back the virus directly. That distinction appears to have mattered for some parents, Milner said. Across the region, some parents have been hesitant to get their children vaccinated for certain diseases, amid a national anti-vaccine movement. But Milner has had patients who agree to RSV antibodies for their babies, but deny routine childhood vaccines. “People like the idea that it’s not triggering an immune response,” Milner said, “for whatever reason.” Hardenbrook also has noticed that families who refuse many childhood vaccines will sometimes elect to give their children the RSV immunization. Whereas parents may be less familiar with the devastation caused by measles and polio before vaccination, RSV’s symptoms may be more top of mind. “Almost anybody who has young kids knows somebody who’s had a kid that had RSV that was really sick,” Hardenbrook said. “People know more about it, and know how bad it can be.” Let the news come to you Get any of our free email newsletters — news headlines, sports, arts & entertainment, state legislature, CFD news, and more. (Staff File) By Adejare Atanda and Mfon Elegbede PUBLISHED: October 13, 2026 at 12:12 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... It’s officially fall — the mornings are sharp with cold, and the nights heavy with dew. These are perfect conditions for respiratory viruses to spread as we start to spend more time indoors. During the 2024-25 respiratory virus season, Maryland hospitals admitted 15,000 people with flu, COVID-19 or RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), and more than 1,200 of them unfortunately died. These viruses will return this fall, and we have strong tools to protect ourselves, but people are not getting clear guidance on how to apply these tools. We have updated flu and COVID-19 vaccines, RSV protections for infants and older adults that did not exist five years ago and antiviral medications to help people at high risk. However, health agencies that used to speak with one voice on vaccines are now sending mixed messages or staying silent. This has created a significant amount of uncertainty. According to a recent national survey, many people remain unclear whether specific respiratory vaccines are recommended for them. In April, Gov. Wes Moore signed the Vax Act, which directed the state health secretary to issue Maryland’s own immunization recommendations. These are grounded in the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. It is still too early to know whether this respiratory season will be mild or severe, but now is a great time to get clear on how to protect yourself and your family. Who needs what Flu, COVID-19 and RSV spread in similar ways and can cause many of the same symptoms, but they do not affect everyone equally. For example, flu can affect people of all ages, but children are especially vulnerable. COVID-19 is no longer the emergency it once was, but older adults and people who are immunocompromised still face a higher risk of severe illness. RSV is one that many adults rarely think about, yet it disproportionately affects the youngest and oldest among us. Here is how to think about the risks. If you have a baby at home, think RSV first. For your young kids, consider the flu. If you are 75 and older or immunocompromised, think COVID-19 first, then flu and RSV. And finally, if you are an adult of any age with a chronic disease, all three apply to you. For most households, the guidance for the 2026-27 respiratory virus season is simple enough to fit on an index card: 1. Everyone (6+ months). Annual flu shot, ideally by late October. 2. Adults (19-64). An updated COVID-19 vaccine this fall. 3. Adults (65+). Annual flu shot, plus the two-shot updated COVID-19 vaccine. 4. Adults (50+) with a chronic condition. A one-time RSV vaccine. 5. Pregnant individuals. Annual flu shot, the updated COVID-19 vaccine and an RSV vaccine in the third trimester. 6. Infants. Long-acting RSV antibody shot for infants less than 8 months old who are entering their first respiratory season (if the mother didn’t receive the RSV vaccine during pregnancy) 7. Immunocompromised (any age). Follow the age-appropriate guidelines above, plus an expanded COVID-19 vaccine schedule. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines can all be safely given together at one visit. They may also be given separately, but there is a downside to waiting: Every deferred shot is a shot that may never happen. Vaccines are not the whole prevention strategy Vaccines are the most effective single tool we have to stay protected against these respiratory illnesses, but they are not the entire toolbox. Part of a good plan is knowing what to do when illness arrives. Before you are sick. This is a time-tested preventive measure that is simple but effective: Wash your hands regularly. If you live in a crowded home, good air circulation is key, especially with at-risk groups — newborns, frail older adults, pregnant women and those with immune disorders. Open your windows, run the HVAC fan and consider a portable HEPA filter. In addition, stock up on at-home viral test kits and fitted masks. Finally, keep a list of important phone numbers and addresses handy, including your doctor’s office, urgent care centers and the nearest emergency department. When you get sick. As soon as symptoms start, make those calls and get tested promptly — early treatment is key, depending on the infection — and stay away from at-risk people or mask if you must be around others. Although the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause gives valid federal law priority over conflicting state law, states continue to have broad authority over public health matters, and Maryland has taken advantage of this through the Vax Act to address gaps in federal vaccine guidance. Let’s be clear about what this law does and does not do. It does not create any mandates: Flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines are not required for school, childcare or work, and existing school-entry rules and exemptions remain unchanged. Rather, the law ties two practical allowances to Maryland’s recommendations rather than to federal guidance. Pharmacists can give flu and COVID-19 vaccines without a prescription to anyone 3 years and older. And coverage by state-regulated health plans is tied to the state’s recommendations, so that if federal recommendations narrow, Maryland’s coverage does not have to follow. The insurance protection concern is real. HHS’s latest move could disenfranchise children from lower-income households. Because of federal rules, children covered by Medicaid won’t be able to access vaccines that are no longer recommended by the federal government, even as children with private insurance will. So what should Marylanders actually do? Here are five things: 1. Check vaccine recommendations for your household on the state’s childhood and adult schedules. Your source is health.maryland.gov/recommendedvaccines. When there is conflicting advice or guidance, defer to Maryland’s. 2. If you can, book a single visit. And make that this month. Flu, COVID-19 and RSV shots can be given together. 3. If you are pregnant or expecting a baby this winter, discuss RSV with your doctor now. The window to receive the maternal RSV vaccine is narrow. If needed, check with your pediatrician’s office about availability of the RSV antibody for your infant. 4. If you are older, especially with a chronic condition, request the RSV vaccine. Age and chronic conditions are qualifying in Maryland. 5. Make a sick-day plan in advance. This should include telephone numbers and physical addresses of clinicians and telehealth services for when you get sick. With flu activity rising earlier than usual in parts of the country and COVID-19 still elevated, this is a good time to move vaccinations off your “I’ll get around to it” list. Marylanders already do better than most of the country. In 2024-25, 63% of Maryland children and 74% of Marylanders older adults were vaccinated against flu, roughly 10 points above the national figures. This is encouraging. However, during the same season, more than a third of the state’s children went unprotected, and many older Marylanders eligible for the RSV vaccine never received it. With the possibility of a future “twindemic” or “tripledemic” caused by high cases of flu, COVID-19 or RSV that could overwhelm healthcare systems and resources, it is critical for all of us to do our part. The viruses are ones we know, and the tools are better than they have ever been. Maryland has drawn the roadmap, but the rest is up to us. Protect yourself, protect your family and go get those shots. Dr. Adejare Atanda is a health policy researcher and former infectious disease epidemiologist at the Maryland Department of Health. Dr. Mfon Elegbede is a pediatrician and public health expert. Both are Maryland residents. Blue Lake Biotechnology To Present Data For RSV Vaccine Candidate BLB201 In A Late-Breaking Presentation At ISV Annual Congress PR Newswire Mon, October 12, 2026 at 5:59 AM PDT 2 min read ATHENS, Ga. and SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Blue Lake Biotechnology, Inc., a clinical-stage intranasal vaccine company developing parainfluenza virus 5 (PIV5)-vectored vaccines that harness the full breadth of the immune system to protect against serious infectious diseases, today announced that interim data from the company's Phase 1/2a pediatric clinical trial of RSV vaccine candidate BLB201 will be presented as a late-breaking abstract during the International Society for Vaccines 2026 Annual Congress in Antwerp, Belgium. The oral presentation will include updated safety and immunogenicity data from both RSV-seronegative and RSV-seropositive children ranging in age from eight to 59 months. Presentation Details Title: PIV5-vectored Intranasal RSV Vaccine is Safe and Immunogenic in Infants and Young Children Date/Time: October 12, 2026 17:20 CET Presenter: Biao He, Ph.D., CEO, Blue Lake Biotechnology About RSV and BLB201 Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a highly contagious virus that infects over 64 million people worldwide each year. While RSV typically causes mild, cold-like symptoms, it can cause severe and potentially life-threatening disease in infants, older adults, the immunocompromised, and people with certain chronic health conditions. In the U.S., RSV causes up to 80,000 hospitalizations among children under five and up to 160,000 among older adults annually, with up to 10,000 deaths. BLB201 is an intranasal RSV vaccine candidate being evaluated in Phase 1/2a clinical testing in children ages eight to 59 months. Interim data have indicated that BLB201 may prevent symptomatic RSV infection in young children. BLB201 has received Fast Track designation from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for prevention of RSV-associated acute respiratory disease in adults over 60 and pediatric populations. BLB201 uses a proprietary PIV5 vector to express the RSV-F protein. PIV5 has been used for decades in canine vaccines and is not known to cause human disease. About Blue Lake Biotechnology Blue Lake Biotechnology, Inc. and affiliate CyanVac LLC are developing intranasal vaccines designed to activate mucosal, systemic, and cellular immunity. Our proprietary PIV5 platform mimics natural infection while expressing proteins from targeted pathogens. Our clinical-stage pipeline includes vaccines designed to prevent respiratory infections and overcome limitations of existing vaccine technologies. Learn more at Blue Lake Biotechnology. Women's Health Innovation Giving Find a Doctor Search Share Bloomington, Illinois, October 09, 2026 | 08:27 AM America/Chicago RSV vaccine offers protection for people at risk Summary Key Takeaways: The RSV virus can cause severe respiratory illness, hospitalization, and even death, especially in infants and older adults. RSV vaccination is recommended for adults 75 and older, and some adults ages 50–74 with higher-risk health conditions. Pregnant women or newborns can receive preventive protection during RSV season, helping reduce the risk of severe illness. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) often looks like a common cold, but it’s a virus that can have much more serious consequences, especially for babies and older adults. A vaccine offers protection for people at greatest risk. And for older people, it can be a one-time shot rather than an annual vaccination. Talha Khan, MD, a family medicine physician at OSF HealthCare, says RSV is a common respiratory virus that can affect people of all ages. Young infants and older adults are among those most likely to develop severe illness. “It can cause pretty severe respiratory infection that can lead to hospitalization and even death, so it is something we don’t take lightly. And we do have a vaccine for it now. So we do recommend getting that vaccine, if they’re eligible, so they have that extra layer of protection.” For adults, the RSV vaccine is recommended for everyone age 75 and older. “It can be given to individuals who are younger than that – age 50 to 74 – if they have some chronic conditions: respiratory disease, things like COPD, asthma, heart disease and if they’re a current smoker. All those things put them at increased risk for a more severe infection.” For infants, RSV can be particularly dangerous during the virus’s typical fall and winter season. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention points out it is the number one cause of hospitalization among infants in the U.S. The RSV vaccine can offer preventive protection when given to the baby after birth. “And then it’s also recommended for pregnant women if they’re pregnant during that respiratory virus season [September-January], as well. They recommend either pregnant women get it or the infant gets it once their born, typically not both.” During a particularly bad respiratory virus season in 2022, OSF OnCall launched a free, at-home monitoring service for babies and toddlers up to five years old. The digital service continues today and includes an at-home care kit and easy access to a real-time chat. If necessary, a video visit is an option for parents or guardians of an infant or young child with any respiratory illness, including RSV. While RSV is common, many older adults may not be as familiar with the vaccine as they are with annual flu or COVID-19 shots. “A few of my patients have kind of brought up that, ‘Oh, that’s one of the vaccines I’ve never heard of,’” says Dr. Khan. “But, again, it is important because it can cause those severe respiratory infections, [including] pneumonia, and potentially even lead to death. So, if we can stop that or stop you from getting a serious infection with a one-time vaccine, then why not just get that done.” For people who may qualify for the vaccine, health providers recommend talking with a health care professional about their individual risk factors and the best way to protect against severe RSV. With a single dose offering long-term protection, the decision may be one that is easier to make than most people realize. Dr. Talha Khan is a family medicine physician at OSF HealthCare in Bloomington, Illinois. Maternal vaccination with RSVpreF (Abrysvo) protects newborns from getting the virus, yet relatively few moms in the United States and Europe have opted for it since its rollout in 2023, a study published last week in The Lancet Regional Health-Europe finds. “We found the vaccine reduced the risk of RSV-related hospitalization in babies under six months by around 74%, which lines up well with what the clinical trials predicted,” senior author Ting Shi, PhD, MPH, of the University of Edinburgh’s Usher Institute, said in a university news release. “But uptake during the first vaccination seasons was low.” 19% to 50% vaccine uptake Researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the University of Granada in Spain led the study, which examined data from 16 studies from the United States, the United Kingdom, and France. The studies included more than 4 million pregnancies in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Thirteen studies took place in the United States, where 27.1% of pregnant women accepted the maternal RSV vaccine. One cross-sectional study in England showed a 19% maternal RSV vaccine uptake, while a study in Scotland indicated 50.4% of women received the dose. The French study showed that the rate of acceptance among moms-to-be was about the same as it was in the United States: 27.2%. Women who received other vaccines recommended during pregnancy were more likely to accept the RSVpreF vaccine, which works best if administered from 32 to 36 weeks’ gestation. We found the vaccine reduced the risk of RSV-related hospitalization in babies under six months by around 74%, which lines up well with what the clinical trials predicted. Ting Shi, PhD, MPH The scientists also looked at data about how well the RSV vaccine worked and discovered that it was 73.6% effective against hospitalization for babies 6 months or younger. “Research shows that RSV vaccination during pregnancy protects babies,” Evelyn Balsells, PhD, MPH, of the University of Granada, said in the news release. “Efforts to increase uptake and reduce disparities will be essential to maximize the benefits of maternal RSV vaccination.” Need for proactive rather than reactive strategy An accompanying editorial addressed low vaccine coverage in the European Union and the need to bolster maternal vaccination rates across the continent. “Maternal vaccination protects infants during the most clinically vulnerable first months, before they are eligible for routine childhood vaccinations, but uptake of many maternal vaccines remains low despite strong evidence of efficacy and safety,” the authors wrote. The authors suggested several strategies, including better coordination among medical specialties when it comes to recommending and providing vaccines, outreach to areas where structural barriers lead to low vaccination rates, better surveillance of diseases and vaccine coverage, and a proactive instead of reactive vaccine strategy. “Europe should not wait for the next maternal vaccine to be licensed before addressing these systemic weaknesses,” they added.
